indian-startups-7a4714c2b7.headline: Indian startup funding nosedives 47.5% to $678 Mn in October
indian-startups-7a4714c2b7.fulltext:
Indian startups raised $678 million in October, a 47.5% month-on-month decline, as the absence of large funding rounds dragged overall investments. No startup secured a funding round of $100 million or more, while only Tessolve and Even Healthcare crossed the $50 million mark. Growth stage deals received a boost from rounds raised by Boldfit, DailyObjects, RapidCanvas and Nat Habit, while early stage funding saw moderate participation from Auxo AI, Cent, Mesa and Matiks.
The month saw no reported layoffs, while Jio Platforms made a high-profile stock market debut, followed by listings of Zetwerk and AceVector, the operator of Snapdeal. Merger and acquisition activity, however, remained limited to select sectors.
[Overview]
According to data compiled by Entrackr, Indian startups raised approximately $678 million in funding during October. This amount included 20 growth and late-stage deals totalling $414.6 million, along with 79 early-stage deals worth $263 million. Additionally, there were 9 undisclosed deals during the period.
Y-o-Y and M-o-M trend
October 2026 saw a sharp decline in startup funding compared to the same month last year. Total funding fell 60.8% to $677.8 million from $1.73 billion in October 2025. On a month-on-month basis, funding declined 47.5% from $1.29 billion in September. February was the strongest month for funding in 2026, with startups raising around $2 billion, followed by June, which also recorded around $2 billion. October’s decline came amid a lack of larger deals, with no startup raising $100 million or more during the month.
[Top 10 growth-stage deals]
Growth and late-stage startups saw activity across sectors in October, led by semiconductor solutions provider Tessolve Semiconductor, which raised $75 million, followed by healthtech startup Even Healthcare with $50 million. Sports and fitness brand Boldfit secured $42 million, while lifestyle brand DailyObjects and enterprise AI startup RapidCanvas raised $35 million and $29 million, respectively. Advanced materials manufacturer Simplify raised $25 million, followed by robotics startup Origin with $20 million. Beauty and wellness brand Nat Habit and AI startups Simplismart and Live2.ai raised $15 million, $14 million and $14 million, respectively.
[Top 10 early-stage deals]
Early-stage startups saw funding across AI, healthtech, edtech and gaming in October, led by enterprise AI startup AuxoAI, which raised $20.7 million, followed by healthtech startup Cent with $15 million. Mesa School of Business and Confido Health secured $12.5 million each, while gaming startup Spill Games raised $10.5 million. AI video platform Clueso, quantum computing startup Quanfluence and social gaming platform Matiks received $10 million each. Nutrition brand Ace Blend raised $9.91 million, while edtech startup byteXL secured $9 million to expand its technology training programmes.
[Mergers and acquisitions]
Indian startups recorded five acquisitions in October across SaaS, healthtech, cybersecurity and FMCG. Freshworks acquired AI startup Robusta, while healthtech startup Cent acquired Medsee and cybersecurity firm Protectt.ai acquired AIShield. In the FMCG sector, Marico acquired Satya Nutraceuticals for $110 million. Meanwhile, Hoola Health acquired UpTodd, marking continued consolidation in the healthtech sector.
[City and segment-wise deals]
Bengaluru led startup funding in October with $420 million across 52 deals, accounting for 61.97% of the total capital raised. Delhi-NCR followed with $110.26 million across 18 deals, while Mumbai startups raised $57.53 million across 11 deals. Hyderabad secured $41.22 million across five deals, followed by Bhubaneswar with $11.5 million from a single deal.
E-commerce startups led sector-wise funding with $182.69 million across 27 deals, followed by AI startups with $131.12 million across 22 deals. Healthtech companies raised $104.61 million across 13 deals, while semiconductor startups secured $75 million in a single deal. Manufacturers raised $36.67 million across four deals, rounding out the top five segments.
[Series-wise deals]
Series B startups led funding in October with $209.34 million across 10 deals, followed by Series A companies with $135.35 million across 17 deals. Seed-stage startups raised $80.41 million across 41 deals, while Series C companies secured $61.5 million across three deals. Pre-Series A startups raised $23.24 million across seven deals.
[Key hirings and departures]
October saw key leadership appointments across startups and investment firms, with Mayank Khanduja joining Bessemer Venture Partners as a partner and Manas Poddar taking charge as CBO at OTPless. Sanjeev Bikhchandani continued as MD and group CEO at Info Edge, while Kiran U joined Bellatrix Aerospace as CFO. Other notable appointments included Basant Dhawan as CMO at Shoonya by Finvasia, Medhavi Singh as India country head at Aleph and Kamaldeep Singh as CEO at Infost Energy. Meanwhile, Sanjeev Bikhchandani and Mithun Sacheti were among the key departures, from Info Edge and Nazara Technologies, respectively.
[Tends]
Zorit comeback: Zorit (formerly Bijnis) raised funding from investors including Sparoww Capital and Info Edge Capital, which had written off its entire investment in the startup in 2023.
Vama funding: Spiritual tech startup Vama raised funding from the Dainik Bhaskar family office, which could be among its first recorded startup investments.
Quick home services race: Snabbit recorded an NTV of Rs 72 crore in Q2 FY27, marginally ahead of Urban Company's InstaHelp at Rs 71 crore. Snabbit reported a burn of Rs 142 crore against InstaHelp's adjusted EBITDA loss of Rs 174 crore, although the figures may not be directly comparable.
Burma Burma follows Subway India with IPO filing: Hunger Pangs, the operator of Burma Burma, filed its DRHP for an IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to Rs 600 crore, with no OFS. The filing follows that of Subway India operator EverBrands India in September.
[Conclusion]
October’s funding slowdown reflects a more selective investment environment, with investors prioritising stronger business fundamentals and clearer paths to profitability. Indian startups have raised nearly $11 billion so far in 2026. If funding averages $1 billion in each of the remaining two months, the annual total could cross the $13 billion recorded in 2023. Otherwise, 2026 could end with the lowest annual funding in three years. The coming months will determine whether the slowdown is temporary or signals a prolonged period of cautious investment.

ai-adac3e2890.headline: India proposes AI governance guidelines for telecommunications networks and services
ai-adac3e2890.fulltext:
India proposes AI governance guidelines for telecommunications networks and services
New draft guidelines in India propose safeguards for the responsible use of AI in telecommunications networks and services.
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released draft guidelines on the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in telecommunications networks and services. Published on 30 October 2026, the proposal seeks to establish governance and accountability requirements for telecommunications operators deploying AI systems. Stakeholders can submit comments until 27 November 2026.
According to the Ministry of Communications, telecommunications networks support essential public services, economic activities, critical information infrastructure, national security, and emergency response. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into network operations and service provision, the regulator considers sector specific guidance necessary to ensure its responsible deployment. The initiative seeks to provide greater regulatory clarity and accountability while adapting India’s broader AI Governance Guidelines, published in February 2026, to the particular characteristics and risks of telecommunications infrastructure.
The draft guidelines would apply to authorised entities providing telecommunications services or operating telecommunications networks that use or intend to use AI systems. They would require operators to establish internal AI governance policies, classify AI systems according to their potential risks, and introduce human oversight mechanisms. Operators would also need to conduct validation, conformity, and impact assessments before deploying or modifying AI systems.
The proposal also introduces requirements for recording, investigating, and mitigating AI-related incidents, including reporting critical and high-severity incidents to TRAI. Operators would be required to establish an AI Governance and Safety Committee, implement data governance safeguards, and maintain mechanisms for addressing consumer complaints related to AI systems. They would remain accountable for the outcomes of AI systems, including those developed or supplied by third parties.
Why does it matter?
AI is increasingly used to manage and optimise telecommunications networks, potentially improving efficiency and service quality while introducing risks to network reliability, cybersecurity, and service continuity. Failures or unintended behaviour in AI systems supporting critical network functions could affect connectivity and the delivery of essential services. The proposed guidelines seek to address these risks through sector specific requirements for risk assessment, human oversight, and incident management.
The proposal also addresses accountability as telecommunications operators increasingly rely on AI technologies supplied by third parties. By requiring operators to assess these systems and remain responsible for their outcomes, TRAI seeks to strengthen oversight throughout their deployment and operation. The consultation will help determine how these safeguards are implemented and how operators balance network innovation with security, resilience, and consumer protection.

indian-startups-7eb438ef2b.headline: Pixxel Is Indian-Owned And Controlled, Says Founder Amid Backlash Over US Foray
indian-startups-7eb438ef2b.fulltext: Bengaluru-based spacetech soonicorn Pixxel’s founder and CEO Awais Ahmed has dismissed questions over the startup’s Indian ownership and control following online criticism over the launch of its US subsidiary, Pixxel Federal. In a post on X, Ahmed said Pixxel remains headquartered, owned, managed, and controlled in India, rejecting allegations questioning its corporate structure and national credentials. “First, Pixxel is Indian-HQed, Indian owned, Indian-managed and Indian-controlled,” he said, adding that its primary Indian entity was incorporated in 2018, before any of its international entities. Ahmed said the Indian entity is not a subsidiary of a US company and remains the primary vehicle for executing Pixxel’s Indian government, space, and defence programmes. Pixxel Federal’s board and CEO would have authority only over the US subsidiary and its operations, with no control over the startup’s Indian government programmes or domestic business, he added. The clarification follows Pixxel’s announcement that it had established Pixxel Federal to pursue US government contracts across civilian, defence, and intelligence agencies. Pixxel’s Ownership Structure Ahmed said Pixxel has faced targeted social media attacks, anonymous emails to government customers, and attempts to cast doubt on its ownership, technology, and credentials. Addressing its shareholding, he said Indian investors, including the founders, collectively hold the largest share by percentage, followed by investors from Singapore, the UK, and the US. No international investor has unilateral control over Pixxel beyond customary investor protections, he added. Ahmed also said intellectual property developed for Indian government projects remains under Indian ownership and control, with these programmes executed through Indian entities and governed by Indian laws. He said Pixxel’s overseas presence predates Pixxel Federal, with its existing US entity incorporated a few months after the Indian company in 2018 to serve American and international customers. Pixxel plans to set up entities in more countries as it expands globally. “We intend to build a global space company rooted in Indian engineering. That means selling Indian technology worldwide, hiring internationally, establishing local entities where required, and complying with each country's laws,” he said. The CEO said separate entities are necessary in regulated sectors such as space and defence to meet national security, export control, licensing, and customer confidentiality requirements. “Having one entity isn't some extraordinary achievement in governance, and having several isn't evidence of questionable patriotism,” he said. He added that Pixxel plans to go public in India in a few years, when its complete corporate structure would be disclosed for public scrutiny. Ahmed’s response follows comments by fellow Bengaluru-based spacetech startup GalaxEye, which said it consciously chose to remain headquartered in India despite considering other locations. In a post on X, GalaxEye said its founders and investors had decided to build the business from India. It also highlighted its single-entity corporate structure, saying all its contracts and bids had been pursued through GalaxEye. “Every contract and every bid we have applied for has come from a single entity: GalaxEye. We have kept our corporate structure simple and our governance clean,” it said. Without naming any company, GalaxEye referred to the practice of setting up multiple entities across jurisdictions to qualify for and secure projects, saying it had chosen not to follow that approach. “That discipline has a cost in the short term. We believe it pays back in trust, and trust is what a space company is ultimately built on,” it added. Pixxel Expands Its Government Business Founded by Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal, Pixxel develops hyperspectral imaging satellites that capture data across multiple narrow wavelength bands, revealing details on the Earth’s surface that conventional satellite imagery may miss. Its new subsidiary, Pixxel Federal, will offer Earth observation technologies, satellite mission systems, and geospatial intelligence services to US government agencies. It also plans to establish an office near Washington, DC, to work more closely with government customers and partners. The expansion builds on Pixxel’s existing engagements with NASA and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), including a contract under NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme and an NRO Strategic Commercial Enhancements contract. In September, Pixxel raised $100 Mn in a Series C funding round co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, taking its total funding to around $195 Mn. In India, a Pixxel-led consortium is developing a 12-satellite Earth observation constellation under a public-private initiative with IN-SPACe.

health-tech-46221ec196.headline: STAT+: FDA OKs generic HIV prevention shot, widening access for lower-income countries
health-tech-46221ec196.fulltext:
After months of anticipation, the Food and Drug Administration gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version of a groundbreaking HIV prevention medicine, a key step in widening access for dozens of low- and middle-income countries.
The company, one of the world’s largest generic drugmakers, plans to start shipping the medicine next month as part of an effort propelled, in part, by several global health organizations to ensure the drug becomes available in lower-income countries as quickly as possible. The annual cost per person will be $40, comparable to daily tablets.
Known as lenacapavir, the injectable drug is widely seen as a game-changing tool for eradicating HIV because it offers virtually complete protection against contracting the virus with just one administration every six months. The brand-name version, which is known as Yetzugo in the U.S., is marketed by Gilead Sciences and was approved by the FDA last year.

ai-28ccca4d43.headline: Cohere Targets CAD $7 Billion Series E Funding to Accelerate Sovereign AI
ai-28ccca4d43.fulltext:
Cohere, a leading provider of sovereign AI for regulated industries and governments, announced the initial close of its Series E funding round targeting up to CAD $7 billion, which would represent a CAD $35.7 billion valuation.
Commitments to date include the companies of Schwarz Group, one of Europe's largest investors in AI and cloud infrastructure, as the lead investor. New institutional and strategic investors include Bell Ventures, Bullhound Capital and the Government of Canada, while Inovia Capital, NVIDIA and Prosperity7 Ventures are returning investors.
The round marks the largest private financing round ever undertaken by a Canadian technology company and underscores a broader global shift toward sovereign AI. As AI becomes increasingly mission-critical, organizations are seeking independent alternatives that provide greater control over their data, infrastructure, governance, and deployment environments.
Cohere has seen rapid growth since launching North, its agentic AI platform, ending Q3 2026 with 165% year-over-year ARR growth, driven by new customer wins and expansions across commercial and public sector organizations. Over the past year, Cohere has increased its global customer base by 20x to 300 customers, reflecting growing adoption with industry leaders across highly regulated industries including Aston Martin Aramco, Bell Canada, Fujitsu, RBC, RWS, PwC, TD Bank, TKMS, and more.
The companies of Schwarz Group are the lead investor and one of the largest investors in European AI and cloud infrastructure, whose IT and digital division Schwarz Digits recently committed billions to next-generation data centre capacity in Germany.
The Government of Canada's equity investment will help Cohere scale from Canada, supporting Canadian jobs and computing infrastructure while giving Canadians a stake in the company's global success. Cohere is making a number of commitments as part of the investment to support Canada's economic vision and grow the country's sovereign AI ecosystem.
Aidan Gomez, CEO and Co-Founder, Cohere
Today we are announcing the initial close of our Series E, a record-setting round that marks the largest private capital raise in Canadian history. This is a huge honour, not only for Cohere but for the country as the government's investment highlights Canada's leadership in the global AI revolution. Our company is one of the few building artificial intelligence that is changing the world. For our proud home of Canada, its global standing, and its international leadership, we are celebrating something historic.
Francois Chadwick, Chief Financial Officer, Cohere
Cohere will use the funding to advance our modelling and product roadmap, develop fully verticalized AI solutions for regulated industries, and invest in long–term compute infrastructure needed to train frontier–level enterprise models. We will continue to meaningfully scale across North America, EMEA, and APAC to meet growing customer demand.
Christian Müller, CEO, Schwarz Digits
The companies of Schwarz Group are proud to lead Cohere's Series E investment at a pivotal moment for AI, where digital sovereignty has become a strategic imperative for global competitiveness. Digital sovereignty is about strategic choice, interoperability and holding the keys to our own data. Following the strategic business combination of Cohere and Aleph Alpha, this investment marks the next logical milestone on a roadmap that we have methodically built: uniting European research excellence and explainability with global enterprise scale. Our partnership brings together Canadian AI leadership and trusted European infrastructure, giving customers greater choice and control over how they deploy secure AI. Our clear goal is to anchor these frontier capabilities in our sovereign STACKIT cloud infrastructure. We are excited to support its continued growth across Europe and around the world.

climate-energy-3f56c6e85c.headline: India's emissions growth slows as renewable energy begins replacing coal, UNEP report finds
climate-energy-3f56c6e85c.fulltext:
- India’s greenhouse gas emissions broke from a longer period of rapid growth in 2025, according to UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026. However, different datasets disagree on whether emissions increased or declined slightly.
- Renewable electricity generation increased by 98 terawatt-hours in 2025, nearly twice the increase in electricity demand, while coal-fired generation declined by 44 terawatt-hours.
- Milder weather and slower electricity demand growth also contributed to the slowdown. Researchers caution that sustained emissions reductions will require greater investment in energy storage, transmission and industrial decarbonisation.
The upward trend of greenhouse gas emissions in India showed a significant change in 2025. The trend, which was indicating a longer period of rapid growth, has pivoted from this path and is now showing a slight decline in India’s emissions. This has been reported in the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) new report Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, released on October 21.
The report finds that the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) and the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicate a slight decline in India’s emissions, while the Energy Institute estimates a marginal increase. However, all three indicate a departure from the country’s earlier pattern of rapid emissions growth, partly because of weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy.
“The data this year is very encouraging,” said Minal Pathak, a researcher at Ahmedabad University and a lead author of the UNEP report’s chapter on global emissions trends, in a written response to Mongabay-India.
She said the change was partly attributable to weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy, as highlighted in Chapter 2 of the report.
India remains the world’s third-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China and the United States. Its emissions reached approximately 4.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2025, excluding land use and forestry. However, its per capita emissions of 3.1 tonnes were less than half the global average of 6.4 tonnes.
A separate analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), published by Carbon Brief, estimated that India’s CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and cement increased by just 0.7% in 2025, the slowest growth since 2001, excluding the pandemic year of 2020.
The CREA estimate covers fossil-fuel and cement CO₂ emissions, whereas UNEP considers a broader range of greenhouse gases and emissions sources. The figures are therefore not directly comparable.
Renewable electricity generation outpaces demand
India’s renewable electricity generation increased by approximately 98 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026.
Solar generation increased by 53 TWh, or 37%, while wind added 22 TWh and hydropower approximately 21 TWh. During the same period, electricity demand increased by 49 TWh, or 2.4%, compared with 6.2% growth in 2024.
Meanwhile, coal-fired electricity generation declined by 44 TWh, or 2.9%. Coal’s share of electricity generation fell from approximately 75% in 2024 to 71% in 2025.
Vaibhav Chaturvedi, a researcher at the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) and a contributing author of Chapter 4 of the UNEP report, said the figures indicate a potentially important change.
“The 2025 figures suggest that renewables are beginning to displace coal rather than simply meet new demand. But this is an emerging shift, and adding clean energy capacity alone will not sustain it unless the power sector can store, transmit and use clean electricity when and where it is needed,” he said in a written response to Mongabay-India.
For the first time, solar overtook hydropower to become India’s largest individual source of clean electricity. Solar supplied approximately 9.4% of India’s electricity in 2025, while solar and wind together contributed around 14%.
All clean sources, including renewables and nuclear energy, accounted for approximately 27% of total electricity generation, compared with around 22% in 2024.
Despite this expansion, coal remained India’s dominant electricity source. According to Ember, coal generation was still 46% higher in 2025 than in 2015.
The reduction in coal generation also affected emissions. Ember estimates that electricity-sector greenhouse gas emissions declined by 2.9%, from 1,437 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2024 to 1,395 million tonnes in 2025.
Weather contributed to weaker electricity demand
Favourable weather conditions also influenced India’s emissions trend.
According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) Statement on the Climate of India during 2025, India’s average temperature was 0.28°C above the 1991–2020 average, compared with an anomaly of 0.65°C in 2024, the warmest year on record.
Although 2025 was still India’s eighth warmest year since 1901, the relatively milder summer reduced electricity demand for cooling.
Ember estimates that lower cooling demand reduced electricity consumption by approximately 32 TWh compared with what would otherwise have been expected.
India also received approximately 1,274 millimetres of rainfall, equivalent to 110% of its long-period average. Southwest monsoon rainfall reached 108% of normal, supporting hydropower generation.
“India’s emissions growth slowed sharply in 2025, and two things explain much of it: a helpful turn in the weather, and the steady rise of clean energy,” Chaturvedi said.
“Such favourable conditions may not recur, and the benefit cannot be regarded as a long-term trend,” he cautioned.
A CREA assessment attributed 44% of the reversal in coal- and gas-fired electricity generation growth, compared with the 2019–2024 trend, to increased clean electricity generation. Another 36% was attributed to reduced cooling demand and 20% to a longer-term slowdown in electricity demand growth unrelated to weather.
These percentages describe the reversal relative to the earlier power-demand trend, not shares of India’s total emissions reductions.
Pathak cautioned against drawing direct conclusions about causes from emissions figures alone.
“We look at data on fuels and emissions, so it is difficult to infer the reason directly from emissions data,” she said.
Industrial production presents a different picture
While electricity-sector emissions declined, India’s steel and cement production continued expanding.
According to CREA’s analysis, steel production increased by approximately 8% in 2025, while cement production grew by around 10%. Together, these industries accounted for approximately 21% of India’s CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and industrial processes.
Growth in emissions associated with steel and cement partly offset reductions from electricity generation and weaker natural gas consumption.
However, some industrial fuels showed declining consumption. Natural gas demand fell by approximately 4%, while demand for petroleum products such as naphtha and petroleum coke also weakened.
“We also see a decline in fossil fuel consumption in industry sectors,” Pathak said.
Changes in industrial production and fossil-fuel consumption do not necessarily follow identical patterns, particularly when industries change fuel sources.
Chaturvedi highlighted the longer-term challenge of reducing industrial emissions while meeting rising energy demand.
“Expansion of renewable energy is a structural change; favourable weather is temporary, and electricity demand is likely to grow as industrial activity, urbanisation and cooling needs increase,” he said.
Can India sustain the decline in coal generation?
Sustaining the shift towards cleaner electricity will require changes beyond renewable energy capacity additions.
India’s electricity system continues to rely heavily on coal, particularly when solar and wind generation is unavailable. Storage, transmission infrastructure and more flexible electricity demand will be important as renewable generation expands.
Chaturvedi identified three priorities, beginning with investment in battery and pumped storage and stronger transmission systems. “First, flexibility must be built alongside capacity, through battery and pumped-storage deployment and stronger transmission, so that clean power generated at one time and place can serve demand at another,” he said.
He also highlighted the importance of electricity pricing.
“Time of day tariffs would encourage consumers to shift use towards periods of high solar and wind output, helping demand and supply match better and lowering system costs,” he said.
The third priority involves aligning electricity planning with the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, alongside specific measures for emissions-intensive sectors such as steel and cement.
Meanwhile, the UNEP report notes that China and India together account for approximately 95% of coal-fired power capacity currently under construction worldwide.
India’s climate targets allow emissions to continue rising
The UNEP report finds that India is likely to meet its 2030 and 2035 emissions-intensity targets under existing policies.
Under its updated nationally determined contribution (NDC), India aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per unit of GDP by 47% relative to 2005 levels by 2035. It also targets approximately 60% non-fossil installed electricity capacity, conditional on international support, and a cumulative forest and tree-cover carbon sink of 3.5–4 billion tonnes of CO₂e relative to 2005.
However, meeting an emissions-intensity target does not necessarily mean absolute emissions will decline.
UNEP estimates that the annual emissions level implied by India’s 2035 NDC is approximately 1,254 million tonnes of CO₂e higher than that implied by its 2030 commitments.
Chaturvedi said India’s expected ability to meet its targets reflects existing climate policies.
“India is likely to meet its 2035 targets under current policies because considerable climate action is already built into existing policy across sectors. This simply means that India is setting targets it can deliver, rather than hollow pledges,” he said.
The report also highlights India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, expected to initially cover more than 700 million tonnes of CO₂e, and the PM Surya Ghar rooftop solar programme, which recorded more than one million installations during its first year.
Pathak emphasised the need to address energy demand alongside cleaner electricity generation.
“At the same time, demand management is key for India – energy efficiency, lifestyle and behaviour change, urban planning and building design could all contribute to emission reduction in Indian cities,” she said.
Global emissions remain far above climate targets
The UNEP report estimates that global greenhouse gas emissions reached approximately 58.4 billion tonnes of CO₂e in 2025, broadly similar to 2024.
Under current policies, global warming could reach approximately 2.8°C by 2100. Even if countries implement their NDCs and continue similar efforts, warming could reach around 2.6°C.
To follow the report’s lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot pathway, global emissions would need to decline by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025 levels.
Under this scenario, temperatures could peak at approximately 1.7–1.8°C around mid-century before returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100, with around a 50% probability.
For India, the 2025 data indicate a shift in electricity generation, but continued industrial growth and rising energy demand mean sustained national emissions reductions are not assured.

india-667f765571.headline: China to restrict exports of giant tunnel-digging machines; why India could be affected
india-667f765571.fulltext:
China is tightening export controls on construction equipment, including tunnel-boring machines, in a move that could affect India's infrastructure projects and add to concerns over its dependence on Chinese machinery.
The new restrictions cover specialised equipment used to build tunnels for roads, railways and metro networks, as well as machines designed to spray concrete at high altitudes.
Beijing has cited the potential military as well as civilian applications of such equipment, warning that "sensitive countries and regions with disputes with China" will face stricter export rules, Bloomberg reported.
The curbs are particularly significant for India, which is among China's major customers for tunnel-boring equipment and is expanding road and railway infrastructure along the Himalayan border.
The two countries have a longstanding territorial dispute in the region, where India has been building connectivity infrastructure to reduce the time required to mobilise troops.
The latest restrictions are due to take effect later this month, according to Bloomberg. They also cover components, raising concerns not only about fresh procurement but also the maintenance of machinery already in use.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said Beijing increasingly viewed its position as a major global construction equipment producer in strategic terms.
"It raises the risks of dependency, and incentivizes other countries to try to de-risk from China," Chan said.
Why the restrictions matter for India
China accounts for around 70% of the global tunnel-boring machine market, according to Chinese state media figures cited by Bloomberg. Its leading manufacturer, China Railway Engineering Equipment Group Co Ltd, says its machinery is used in 36 countries, including Denmark and France.
India has previously faced delays in procuring Chinese-made tunnelling equipment.
In 2024, China delayed efforts by German manufacturer Herrenknecht AG to sell tunnel-boring machines to India for projects including the Ahmedabad-Mumbai bullet train and the Delhi Metro.
A spokesperson for Herrenknecht said the company was studying the latest Chinese restrictions.
The new controls could also affect the supply of spare parts. Ajay Srivastava, founder of the New Delhi-based Global Trade Research Initiative, said India could shift equipment between priority projects if necessary, but restrictions on components could create difficulties for existing machinery.
"When there is heavy wear and tear in these machines we require regular supply of parts," Srivastava said, adding that the curbs could affect both the existing stock of machines and the procurement of new ones.
The inclusion of equipment used for concrete spraying at high altitudes has also drawn attention. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing, said this could indicate a particular focus on "strategically sensitive terrain".
"For China, the central concern is where Chinese engineering capabilities are used and whether they could strengthen another country's military infrastructure," Sun said.
India looks to reduce dependence on Chinese machinery
The restrictions come as India seeks to expand domestic manufacturing of high-value construction and infrastructure equipment.
The government is considering a $1.2-billion incentive scheme for manufacturers of equipment such as tunnel-boring machines, firefighting systems and elevators.
The proposed programme is expected to attract around $1.8 billion in fresh investment by offering incentives to domestic manufacturers over seven years. It is also expected to include local value-addition targets for machinery that is currently imported.
The scheme was announced in the 2026-27 Union Budget as part of efforts to strengthen domestic production of technologically advanced construction and infrastructure equipment. State-run BEML, along with private-sector companies such as Larsen & Toubro and Johnson Lifts, could benefit from the proposed incentives, according to the earlier report.
India's infrastructure expansion is expected to drive demand for specialised equipment. Road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari has said the country aims to invest up to $9.6 billion in tunnelling over the next five years and has urged domestic industry to manufacture tunnel-boring machines.
Domestic manufacturing faces cost challenges
Larsen & Toubro, one of India's major engineering companies, is working on developing its own tunnel-boring machine.
R Shankar Raman, president of the Mumbai-based company, said L&T was building a prototype and could eventually manufacture machinery for its own projects and other buyers if the experiment proved successful.
However, he cautioned that India's manufacturing industry was still at an earlier stage, while Chinese manufacturers benefited from large-scale production.
"If people are still going to compare with Chinese price and find ways to import from China," Raman said, "then India will be at a disadvantage."
Bloomberg Economics said the restrictions could slow some infrastructure projects, including strategic construction along the disputed Himalayan border.
However, it also noted that tighter Chinese export controls could strengthen India's case as an alternative manufacturing base, encouraging foreign equipment makers to add capacity in the country.
Besides Herrenknecht, manufacturers in the US and Japan also produce potential alternatives to Chinese tunnelling equipment. However, switching suppliers in the short term could be difficult for customers that rely heavily on Chinese machinery.

ai-19ce29ebfa.headline: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
ai-19ce29ebfa.fulltext:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.
Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).
Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.
The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.
Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.
With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.
Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.
The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.
Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.
Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. It considers Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, a direct competitor, along with Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, which helps companies build and train their own AI agents.
Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.
Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

indian-startups-2ca2d052d2.headline: India's startup funding slows as global investors turn cautious, capital shifts to US
indian-startups-2ca2d052d2.fulltext:
India's startup funding market is undergoing a correction, with late-stage and angel investments declining sharply as global investors turn more selective and redirect capital towards other markets and sectors.
Rupee depreciation and intensifying competition, particularly from the US, have made fundraising harder for Indian startups and venture capital (VC) funds. Investors are also reassessing valuations and demanding stronger business fundamentals before committing capital.
The slowdown follows an exceptional funding boom in 2020 and 2021, which experts attribute to excessive liquidity and valuations that proved difficult to sustain.
Late-stage funding, which peaked at $29.7 billion in 2021, fell to $6.1 billion in 2025 and $5.7 billion as of 26 October 2026. The number of rounds also declined from 277 in 2021 to 164 in 2025 and 98 so far in 2026, according to Tracxn data.
“As interest rates normalized, capital rebalanced and the market reset to levels that fundamentals could support. What has changed is the underwriting discipline. The anchor is now public-market comparables, which means positive unit economics, a clear path to profitability, improving contribution margins and cash conversion,” said Karan Mohla, general partner at global multi-stage venture capital firm B Capital, where he leads the South and Southeast Asia team.
Analysts view the decline as a re-baselining of the ecosystem. The 2021 peak was driven by the zero interest rate policy (ZIRP) era, when abundant capital flowed into late-stage private rounds at forward revenue multiples that public markets were unlikely to sustain.
A changing landscape
A shift in investor appetite is adding to the slowdown. While funds earlier backed conventional financial services and internet businesses, interest has increasingly moved towards artificial intelligence (AI) and deeptech. Many companies in these sectors, however, are still too young to attract late-stage investments.
“My sense is that late-stage funding will pick up around 2028, when these companies mature and graduate to that stage. Until then, some companies in the consumer and financial services sectors will continue to attract late-stage capital. However, the investment landscape is undergoing a reset, with a shift in the kinds of businesses investors find attractive,” said Ashish Kumar, co-founder and general partner at venture capital firm Fundamentum and F2A (Fundamentum Frontier Advisors).
Between 2020 and 2026 YTD, retail, enterprise applications and fintech attracted the most funding, at $32.2 billion, $31.5 billion and $25.6 billion, respectively, Tracxn data showed.
The retreat of once-active growth-stage investors has further constrained capital flows. Tiger Global's investments in Indian startups fell from 55 in 2021 to one in 2026 YTD. SoftBank, which made 17 investments in 2021, largely stayed away from fresh deals after 2022 before making two investments in 2026, according to Venture Intelligence.
Global capital looks elsewhere
Competition from the US has added to the pressure, with global investors increasingly concentrating capital in artificial intelligence. Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have raised billions of dollars at multi-billion-dollar valuations. SpaceX's entry into public markets through its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) in June has added to the pull of the US technology market.
“As a result, there is little incentive for an LP to invest in VC funds in India right now. India has become a classic high-potential but underperforming market for global LPs,” said Abhay Agarwal, founder and fund manager of early-stage VC firm Piper Serica Advisors.
The pullback extends to the earliest stages of startup financing. Angel funding ffell from $542 million in 2020 to $95.4 million in 2025, while the number of rounds declined from 577 to 286, according to Traxcn data.
Experts attribute the decline partly to the growing institutionalisation of angel investing. Angel networks are increasingly setting up their own funds, tapping domestic capital to formalise early-stage investments in the startup ecosystem, Mint reported in March.
Regulatory changes have added to the uncertainty. Under revisions to the Securities and Exchange Board of India's (Sebi) accredited investor framework, angel funds can raise capital only from accredited investors and must onboard at least five such investors before their first close. Investors must meet prescribed income or net-worth criteria and undergo accreditation.
The changes have raised concerns that smaller and newer fund managers could struggle to raise capital, as the requirements narrow the pool of eligible investors. Following industry representations, Sebi extended the compliance deadline for existing angel funds from 8 September 2026 to 31 March 2027.
However, some industry participants argue that tighter regulations may change how angel capital is deployed rather than reduce its overall availability.
“If getting accredited is too onerous or the eligible pool shrinks too much, you'll see capital simply route around the regulated structure — people will invest directly or find other vehicles. So the regulation may end up reshaping the pipeline more than shrinking the overall pool,” said Nidhi Killawala, partner at law firm Khaitan & Co.

indian-startups-061e50c4dc.headline: Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West
indian-startups-061e50c4dc.fulltext:
A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.
Highly capable, low-cost Chinese open-weight models see widespread adoption, yet Western enterprises fear censorship, cybersecurity risks, and geopolitical bias.
Startups see business opportunities in editing the models to strip state propaganda and security flaws for Western markets.
The concept of machine unlearning — or removing data from an artificial intelligence system after it has been trained — was largely an academic pursuit when Ben Luria, an Israeli entrepreneur, co-founded his startup. Then, China’s DeepSeek launched its first open-weight large language model last year, and Luria immediately saw the business potential of realigning it to Western values.
A slew of Chinese open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.AI, Alibabai, and Tencenti have won over users — including American businesses and startups — with their lower costs, strong capabilities, and customization options. Others fear the models are too aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, and that they are not as safe as closed systems.
“We’re not making the model anti-Chinese. We are bringing it up to speed on safety and to the standard of mainstream Western AI.”
“What we’re trying to do is find a way to de-risk the adoption of open-weight models,” Luria, co-founder and chief executive of AI safety startup Hirundo, told Rest of World. “What we do is like neurosurgery, an intervention that’s surgical and very specific. It is to realign the values, geopolitical perceptions, censorship, and state-aligned bias and propaganda to what American and Western companies expect from models they deploy in their workflows.”
Luria’s team edits the weights of open models to harden them and make them more secure against cyberattacks, increase their fairness, and reduce their dangerous knowledge of, for example, bio weapons, he said.
Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike’s analysis of DeepSeek’s R1 model last year showed that prompts containing topics the Chinese government considers politically sensitive were up to 50% more likely to receive code with “severe security vulnerabilities.” Another study found that Chinese models produced less secure code when the user identified as a member of the U.S. government.
Hirundo’s own analysis of Alibaba’s Qwen models showed they do not acknowledge politically sensitive topics in China such as the violent crackdown on protests at Tiananmen Square in 1989 and Hong Kong in 2019, or the existence of forced labor camps in Xinjiang. They also don’t engage on prompts about Winnie the Pooh, possibly because dissidents have used the cartoon character to refer to Premier Xi Jinping.
Hirundo’s realignment ensures Chinese open models give “the balanced perspective” that OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude give, Luria said.
“We’re not making the model anti-Chinese,” he said. “We are bringing it up to speed on safety and to the standard of mainstream Western AI.”
The top Chinese models lag behind the leading closed systems of U.S. frontier labs by just 3% on benchmark scores, and account for the biggest share of downloads on hosting platform Hugging Face as more developers use them. Companies including Airbnb, Uber, and legal AI firm Harvey have also built proprietary models on top of Chinese models, while Europe is developing its OpenEuroLLM sovereign AI model on Qwen.
Yet concerns remain. In October, the Trump administration barred civilian government agencies from using products or services from DeepSeek, citing a potential threat to national security.
If I were running a product in Taiwan, I would be more concerned. … But if I’m making a product that helps people make a website for their coffee shop, it doesn’t matter.”
Boston-based Lazarus AI, which deploys on-premise AI services for the U.S. government and highly regulated industries, realigned Alibaba’s Qwen models by removing their mandatory censorship. It identified the banned topics from leaked censorship guidelines, then generated prompts related to those topics, and used answers produced by Google’s Gemini Flash to realign the models.
After the intervention, the models were able to give information that was not in the training materials, such as names of pro-democracy activists, suggesting the models had originally learned such knowledge and were suppressed from expressing it, Eric Hartford, former chief scientist at Lazarus AI, told Rest of World.
“In the United States, we have this fear of Chinese models potentially having dangerous behaviors baked into them,” he said. “My goal was to … present these models to enterprises and to highly regulated industries and to have [the models] be palatable for them.”
The company’s ReAligned models, billed as “open-source frontier models without the propaganda,” have been deployed at about a dozen companies in the U.S., Hartford said. But other clients, including government agencies, are reluctant to adopt Chinese models even though they are more capable than the open-weight models from OpenAI and Thinking Machines Lab, which they prefer, he said.
While companies such as Hirundo and Lazarus say their method is effective, aligning a model to so-called Western values or making it universally safe “is an impossible standard,” Oriane Peter, a Ph.D. researcher in AI at King’s College London, told Rest of World.
Alignment is about “steering a model’s output toward a specific desired behavior within a well-defined cultural context and application,” she said.
So anyone using a Chinese model outside China must realign it, “not because Western ideology is inherently safer, or more ethical, but because any model must be adapted to the specific social context and environment in which it is meant to operate,” Peter said.
As Chinese open-weight models are widely adopted, there are more tools that claim to uncensor them and remove their refusal mechanisms, a process called abliteration. But many of these tools are not effective, and the models can still retain some of the censorship and misinformation, Luria said.
“It shows that the alignments are deeply embedded, and it’s not that simple to get rid of them.”
Worldwide, there is growing pushback against Western bias in AI systems, with even some Chinese and Russian models defaulting to American geopolitical narratives on historical events, according to researchers. Countries across Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East are developing sovereign AI models to better reflect their languages and culture.
Silicon Valley’s centralized control over model alignment can lead to “a massive homogenization effect” in AI systems, said Peter. This has been linked to cognitive homogenization and intellectual decline among users.
Most users of Chinese models do not care about their alignment, Graham Webster, editor-in-chief of the DigiChina Project at Stanford University, said at a recent Rest of World event.
“If I were running a product in Taiwan, I would be more concerned because it would be throughput that is potentially relevant to the stuff that the Chinese government has enforced strict control over in the training data and the training,” he said. “But if I’m making a product that helps people make a website for their coffee shop, it doesn’t matter.”
Stu Clott, a developer in San Diego, uses DeepSeek for writing, research, and coding tasks. He does not see the need for a realigned model, he told Rest of World.
“I have not had a single situation where censorship got in my way,” he said.
Rina Chandran + is a deputy editor at Rest of World, based in San Francisco.
Viola Zhou + is a reporter for Rest of World covering China's tech scene. She is based in New York City.
Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.
It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.
Chinese open-weight AI models offer high capability at significantly lower costs than U.S. frontier systems, but face monetization and compute challenges, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.
Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.
According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.
It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.
Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

deep-tech-9e885c5449.headline: China’s EDA champion buys start-up to address weak link, support Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law
deep-tech-9e885c5449.fulltext:

Empyrean Technology, China’s top provider of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, plans to acquire a majority stake in a domestic start-up, reinforcing Beijing’s drive for tech self-sufficiency and bolstering support for Huawei Technologies’ semiconductor ambitions.
The Beijing-based firm said in a Shenzhen Stock Exchange filing on Sunday that it would acquire a 50.38 per cent stake in Easy-Logic Technology for 218.8 million yuan (US$33 million). Once completed, the start-up would be consolidated into Empyrean’s financial statements.
Founded in 2021, Shenzhen-based Easy-Logic develops logic optimisation tools that help chip designers reduce iteration time and resource requirements. The start-up’s algorithms had won international EDA competitions and its products were used by nearly 100 digital chip design firms across the globe, according to Empyrean.
The acquisition underscores the urgency of China’s campaign to develop local alternatives to critical foreign technologies. Microchip development relies on EDA software, a market long dominated by three Western players: Synopsys, Cadence Design Systems and Siemens EDA.
As Washington tightens tech export controls on advanced technologies, Beijing has pressed domestic champions – including Empyrean, Primarius Technologies and Semitronix – to close the technological gap with global rivals.
Empyrean noted in the filing that logic optimisation had become increasingly important to chip design as manufacturing processes advanced and the industry adopted Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law.
Unveiled earlier this year, Huawei’s chipmaking methodology aims to achieve transistor performance equivalent to an advanced 1.4-nanometre process node by 2031, reducing reliance on cutting-edge lithography equipment currently blocked by US export curbs.
The framework places higher performance demands on EDA software, creating pressure on domestic suppliers to upgrade their tools.
Empyrean said the acquisition would boost its next-generation artificial intelligence and three-dimensional integrated circuit design (3D IC) capabilities by integrating Easy-Logic’s engineering talent and intellectual property.
The company has emerged as a key backer of Huawei’s road map. In May, Empyrean unveiled Argus, a physical verification platform for 3D IC design that it described as a “key carrier” for implementing the Tau Scaling Law.
Empyrean had also integrated AI-optimised algorithms and agentic tools into its software suite, slashing the time needed for circuit layout tasks from four weeks to one week, chairman Liu Weiping said in September.

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi said India's economic growth has remained high despite the West Asia crisis, whose impact would have been far more serious if the country had not invested in clean energy over the past decade.Commending India's progress in renewable energy sector, he said efforts were on to add 500GW of non-fossil energy capacity over the next 10-11 years. If we continue to remain too dependent on fossil fuels, global economy will continue to be disrupted again and again," he said.Modi said India had already achieved nearly 300GW of non-fossil installed power capacity, accounting for more than 50% of its total capacity, and was pursuing its target of 500GW capacity by 2030.
India's clean energy sector could offer investment opportunities exceeding Rs 20 lakh crore ($220 billion) by the end of the decade as the country expands renewable energy generation, transmission infrastructure, manufacturing and energy storage. More than Rs 15 lakh crore ($164 billion) had been invested in the sector over the past decade, including Rs 6 lakh crore ($63 billion) in the last two years.

climate-energy-69ffef7838.fulltext:
Jaipur: Bhadla Solar Park in 
Rajasthan
, recognised as one of the world’s largest solar power hubs, is set to host India’s first ceramic storage-based concentrated solar power project, supplying solar energy round the clock.
Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Ltd (RRECL) has granted approval to NTPC for setting up a 320-kilowatt pilot CSP project. The project aims to test a new technology that can generate solar power even after sunset, reducing dependence on conventional battery-based energy storage systems.
Under the project, solar energy captured during the day will be stored as heat in specially designed high-temperature ceramic modules. The stored thermal energy will then be used to operate air turbines and generate electricity during nighttime hours. The technology is expected to provide a cost-effective alternative to chemical batteries, which are currently the most common option for storing renewable energy.
The pilot project will use ceramic thermal energy storage technology developed by US-based company 247Solar. “NTPC is implementing the initiative in collaboration with RRECL, with the approval allowing the commencement of feasibility studies, site assessments and structural testing at the Bhadla site,” said an RRECL official.
According to him, all electricity generated from the pilot plant will be used for the internal and auxiliary power requirements of NTPC’s facilities.
While solar parks across the country generate substantial power during daylight hours, providing reliable renewable energy after sunset remains dependent largely on battery storage systems, which involve significant costs.
If the Bhadla pilot proves successful, the technology could open the door for large-scale deployment of ceramic thermal storage systems across India. Such systems have the potential to improve grid reliability while lowering storage costs and reducing dependence on imported battery materials.

global-economics-3a43e6753a.headline: Foreign funds get picky, IPO anchor share hits five-year low
global-economics-3a43e6753a.fulltext:
Foreign investors are growing cautious about India's initial public offerings (IPOs), with their share of anchor investments sliding to a five-year low amid concerns over rich valuations, weak market performance and a global shift in interest towards artificial intelligence (AI). As overseas investors get pickier, domestic institutions are taking on a bigger role, gradually shifting the balance of India’s primary market.
Foreign portfolio investors' (FPI) investments as part of the total anchor book for initial public offerings (IPOs) slumped to its lowest in five years to 36.16% so far this year from its peak of 62.75% in 2021, according to data from PRIME Database. The previous low, as per the data, was 37.85 % in 2022.
FPIs’ share of the total IPO fundraising so far this year has also more than halved from its 2021 level to 11.61%, another five-year low.
The development has led to domestic institutional investors (DIIs) increasingly taking the place of foreign funds in anchor books. Mutual funds, insurance companies and other domestic institutions are emerging as important sources of capital, reducing companies' dependence on overseas investors to raise money.
However, not all issues have been deprived of foreign capital.
“FPIs have continued to participate in larger transactions while being relatively selective about smaller deals," said Dharmesh Anil Mehta, managing director and chief executive officer at DAM Capital Advisors Ltd. "Also, global investors' interest is currently tilted towards AI and technology-related opportunities. India has had relatively fewer such offerings which has also contributed to lower FPI participation.”
Mehta said DIIs now play a much larger role in anchor books, reducing the traditional dependence on foreign institutional capital.
In the anchor book, institutional investors commit funds a day before an IPO opens for subscription. Their participation is closely tracked as it provides an indication of institutional demand and can help build confidence among other investors.
Of the 104 issues that entered the primary market so far in 2026, raising a combined ₹1.55 trillion, anchor investors contributed ₹49,771 crore. FPIs accounted for just ₹17,998 crore of the anchor book, according to PRIME Database. In 2021, companies had raised a total of ₹1.19 trillion. The total anchor book was ₹46,312 crore while FPIs contributed ₹29,059 crore.
Foreign investors are also pulling back from the secondary market. The Nifty 50 has declined around 12% so far this year, weighed down by geopolitical tensions, elevated crude oil prices, rising global bond yields and a stronger US dollar. A weaker rupee, concerns over corporate earnings and relatively expensive valuations have added to the pressure.
FPIs have remained net sellers in Indian equities, with outflows from the equity market amounting to ₹2.95 trillion so far in 2026, according to the data provided by the National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL).
However, their participation in primary markets tells a different story. FPIs recorded net investments of ₹13,239.35 crore in the equity category of 'primary markets and others' in October, a 23% increase from the corresponding period last year. Their cumulative net investments under this category were at ₹68,763.15 crore in 2026 so far, NSDL data showed.
This suggests that foreign investors have not completely turned away from Indian issuances but are being more selective about the companies and valuations they back.
“The composition has evolved significantly, with domestic mutual funds, insurance companies and other institutional investors becoming much larger participants," said Bhavesh A. Shah, managing director at Equirus. "The growth of SIPs (systematic investment plans) and financial savings has created a strong pool of domestic institutional capital.”
Assets managed by mutual funds grew 9.3% to ₹82.64 trillion in September as compared to the same period a year ago. Monthly SIP contributions surged 10.7% to ₹32,490 crore in the same period, according to Association of Mutual Funds in India (Amfi) data.
The growing clout of domestic institutions is also changing how IPOs are prices, giving them a greater say in valuations.
“The dominance of domestic players in IPOs has also led to scaling back of valuations. Domestic institutional investors are better at driving a better price in an IPO, and with the lack of foreign players, such bargaining power has increased,” said Pranav Haldea, managing director of PRIME Database.
“The trend of domestic capital dominating anchor investment is likely to continue as mutual fund flows show no signs of abating,” he added.
Large offerings, however, continue to draw foreign investors' interest. The recent Jio Platforms IPO is expected to turn back their attention to India as the country's largest offering so far. Its anchor book attracted total bids of over $25 billion, or over 30 times the shares available for allocation. Jio Platforms allotted shares worth more than ₹8,100 crore to anchor investors.
Domestic mutual funds got shares worth ₹2,785 crore, accounting for 34.34% of the anchor book, while life insurers and pension funds received ₹1,090 crore, or 13.44%. Overseas investors included BlackRock, Fidelity, Capital Group, JPMorgan Asset Management and Franklin Templeton, along with sovereign investors such as the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
“The Jio Platforms IPO, given its scale and the strength of its underlying business, could be an important catalyst in bringing global investor attention back to the Indian primary market," said Shah. "Ultimately, quality businesses, credible growth prospects and appropriate valuations will attract capital.”
Mehta said the sustained recovery in FPI participation will depend on relative valuations, global liquidity, currency stability and India's attractiveness compared with other emerging markets.

It’s not just rare earths. China is making it harder for other countries to shed their dependence on its solar, drone and drugmaking technology.
They are among the biggest machines in the world: steel cylinders, some as long as a football field, armed with rotating discs that can chew through rock to clear the way for roads and railways. Known as tunnel-boring machines, they are made by only a handful of companies, mostly in factories in China.
India uses them to dig tunnels, including in the Himalayas, to improve its ability to send troops to defend its contested border with China. But starting next month, Beijing is likely to be able to control whether India gets to buy them.
The machines are part of a broader effort by China to control what leaves Chinese factories and laboratories for foreign lands. In the past month, Beijing has moved to control the exports of dozens of technologies, including drones, artificial intelligence models and agents, and certain processes used to develop advanced medicines and to make solar panels.
The overall push could make it much harder for companies in the United States and elsewhere to set up solar energy equipment factories that would compete against Chinese manufacturers. And it could soon make it more difficult for anyone outside China to gain access to the latest and most powerful Chinese A.I. models.
The planned restrictions show that Beijing is doubling down on its strategy of making Chinese factories indispensable to the world, even as many governments are alarmed by their countries’ dependence on China and are pushing to be less reliant.

indian-startups-14b5280c3a.headline: Indian startup funding nosedives 47.5% to $678 Mn in October
indian-startups-14b5280c3a.fulltext:
Indian startups raised $678 million in October, a 47.5% month-on-month decline, as the absence of large funding rounds dragged overall investments. No startup secured a funding round of $100 million or more, while only Tessolve and Even Healthcare crossed the $50 million mark. Growth stage deals received a boost from rounds raised by Boldfit, DailyObjects, RapidCanvas and Nat Habit, while early stage funding saw moderate participation from Auxo AI, Cent, Mesa and Matiks.
The month saw no reported layoffs, while Jio Platforms made a high-profile stock market debut, followed by listings of Zetwerk and AceVector, the operator of Snapdeal. Merger and acquisition activity, however, remained limited to select sectors.
[Overview]
According to data compiled by Entrackr, Indian startups raised approximately $678 million in funding during October. This amount included 20 growth and late-stage deals totalling $414.6 million, along with 79 early-stage deals worth $263 million. Additionally, there were 9 undisclosed deals during the period.
Y-o-Y and M-o-M trend
October 2026 saw a sharp decline in startup funding compared to the same month last year. Total funding fell 60.8% to $677.8 million from $1.73 billion in October 2025. On a month-on-month basis, funding declined 47.5% from $1.29 billion in September. February was the strongest month for funding in 2026, with startups raising around $2 billion, followed by June, which also recorded around $2 billion. October’s decline came amid a lack of larger deals, with no startup raising $100 million or more during the month.
[Top 10 growth-stage deals]
Growth and late-stage startups saw activity across sectors in October, led by semiconductor solutions provider Tessolve Semiconductor, which raised $75 million, followed by healthtech startup Even Healthcare with $50 million. Sports and fitness brand Boldfit secured $42 million, while lifestyle brand DailyObjects and enterprise AI startup RapidCanvas raised $35 million and $29 million, respectively. Advanced materials manufacturer Simplify raised $25 million, followed by robotics startup Origin with $20 million. Beauty and wellness brand Nat Habit and AI startups Simplismart and Live2.ai raised $15 million, $14 million and $14 million, respectively.
[Top 10 early-stage deals]
Early-stage startups saw funding across AI, healthtech, edtech and gaming in October, led by enterprise AI startup AuxoAI, which raised $20.7 million, followed by healthtech startup Cent with $15 million. Mesa School of Business and Confido Health secured $12.5 million each, while gaming startup Spill Games raised $10.5 million. AI video platform Clueso, quantum computing startup Quanfluence and social gaming platform Matiks received $10 million each. Nutrition brand Ace Blend raised $9.91 million, while edtech startup byteXL secured $9 million to expand its technology training programmes.
[Mergers and acquisitions]
Indian startups recorded five acquisitions in October across SaaS, healthtech, cybersecurity and FMCG. Freshworks acquired AI startup Robusta, while healthtech startup Cent acquired Medsee and cybersecurity firm Protectt.ai acquired AIShield. In the FMCG sector, Marico acquired Satya Nutraceuticals for $110 million. Meanwhile, Hoola Health acquired UpTodd, marking continued consolidation in the healthtech sector.
[City and segment-wise deals]
Bengaluru led startup funding in October with $420 million across 52 deals, accounting for 61.97% of the total capital raised. Delhi-NCR followed with $110.26 million across 18 deals, while Mumbai startups raised $57.53 million across 11 deals. Hyderabad secured $41.22 million across five deals, followed by Bhubaneswar with $11.5 million from a single deal.
E-commerce startups led sector-wise funding with $182.69 million across 27 deals, followed by AI startups with $131.12 million across 22 deals. Healthtech companies raised $104.61 million across 13 deals, while semiconductor startups secured $75 million in a single deal. Manufacturers raised $36.67 million across four deals, rounding out the top five segments.
[Series-wise deals]
Series B startups led funding in October with $209.34 million across 10 deals, followed by Series A companies with $135.35 million across 17 deals. Seed-stage startups raised $80.41 million across 41 deals, while Series C companies secured $61.5 million across three deals. Pre-Series A startups raised $23.24 million across seven deals.
[Key hirings and departures]
October saw key leadership appointments across startups and investment firms, with Mayank Khanduja joining Bessemer Venture Partners as a partner and Manas Poddar taking charge as CBO at OTPless. Sanjeev Bikhchandani continued as MD and group CEO at Info Edge, while Kiran U joined Bellatrix Aerospace as CFO. Other notable appointments included Basant Dhawan as CMO at Shoonya by Finvasia, Medhavi Singh as India country head at Aleph and Kamaldeep Singh as CEO at Infost Energy. Meanwhile, Sanjeev Bikhchandani and Mithun Sacheti were among the key departures, from Info Edge and Nazara Technologies, respectively.
[Tends]
Zorit comeback: Zorit (formerly Bijnis) raised funding from investors including Sparoww Capital and Info Edge Capital, which had written off its entire investment in the startup in 2023.
Vama funding: Spiritual tech startup Vama raised funding from the Dainik Bhaskar family office, which could be among its first recorded startup investments.
Quick home services race: Snabbit recorded an NTV of Rs 72 crore in Q2 FY27, marginally ahead of Urban Company's InstaHelp at Rs 71 crore. Snabbit reported a burn of Rs 142 crore against InstaHelp's adjusted EBITDA loss of Rs 174 crore, although the figures may not be directly comparable.
Burma Burma follows Subway India with IPO filing: Hunger Pangs, the operator of Burma Burma, filed its DRHP for an IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to Rs 600 crore, with no OFS. The filing follows that of Subway India operator EverBrands India in September.
[Conclusion]
October’s funding slowdown reflects a more selective investment environment, with investors prioritising stronger business fundamentals and clearer paths to profitability. Indian startups have raised nearly $11 billion so far in 2026. If funding averages $1 billion in each of the remaining two months, the annual total could cross the $13 billion recorded in 2023. Explosions hit Iran’s Qeshm Island as US media report US strikes in Hormuz
Iranian media report several explosions in Qeshm Island and Bandar Lengeh, as US media say the US military carried out the strikes.
Several explosions have been heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island, as media outlets in the United States reported that the US military carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.
The blasts came in rapid succession late on Monday, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz.
The semi-official Fars news agency said explosions were also heard in the port city of Bandar Lengeh, coming from the direction of the sea.
The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that the US military carried out the strikes.
Some officials told the Journal the strikes were defensive, aimed at restricting Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. One official said Washington had deliberately kept the campaign quiet to avoid signalling a return to major combat operations.
The Associated Press news agency also cited a US official as saying the US had conducted defensive strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz. The official said that “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted.
Reporters with Fox News and Axios said the attacks were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing at a US aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Citing a US official, Fox News reporter Jennifer Griffin said the incident did not mark “the start of expanded strikes by the US”.
There was no immediate comment from authorities in Iran or the US.
Earlier on Monday, the IRGC claimed it had captured two US reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm, using electronic warfare systems, and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

They also come amid intensifying diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed US attacks on Iran.
Trump, writing on his Truth Social platform on Monday, suggested that a deal with Iran could happen soon.
