Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei had said Tehran’s demands for peace had been clearly communicated to Washington and “the ball is in the US court”.
He said Iran’s proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz had been condensed and could be implemented within two days if Washington met Tehran’s conditions. These included the US lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports and securing an end to hostilities, paving the way for the reopening of the strait and renewed negotiations.

indian-startups-19ce29ebfa.headline: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
indian-startups-19ce29ebfa.fulltext:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.
Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).
Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.
The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.
Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.
With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.
Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.
The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.
Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.
Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. It considers Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, a direct competitor, along with Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, which helps companies build and train their own AI agents.
Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.
Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

global-economics-55567f8fb8.headline: North Korea Denies Role in $6.3 Billion Binance Crypto Heist

North Korea rejected US claims that it was behind the theft of more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, after the FBI blamed Pyongyang for the biggest crypto heist on record.
The US assertion that North Korea is responsible for the Binance attack is “absurd rhetoric and nothing new,” Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency Tuesday. 
“It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” the statement said, referring to North Korea by its official name.

US authorities have urged crypto exchanges, blockchain operators and other virtual-asset providers to block transactions linked to addresses used to remove the stolen assets.
The Binance hack has sent shockwaves through the crypto industry and has renewed scrutiny of the security risks facing an industry seeking broader acceptance among mainstream investors.

world-0496b26e94.headline: $6B Binance Heist Exposes How North Korea Turned Hacking Into a State Revenue Stream
world-0496b26e94.fulltext:
The FBI blamed Pyongyang for the largest crypto theft on record. Its cash-out routes rely heavily on China.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on October 31 that North Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion in digital assets from Binance – the largest cryptocurrency exchange in the world by trading volume. The FBI labeled the hacking operation behind the attack TraderTraitor.
According to the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs, the attackers moved about $6.36 billion out of the wallets of Binance on 10 blockchains. That would make the theft the largest on record, according to the firm. Most of the money left in about 20 minutes, starting from around 4:00 p.m. U.S. Eastern time on October 29.
Binance said that it had frozen about $3 billion of the stolen assets and it pledged to cover all losses. The company halted withdrawals after the attack, and began a “phased resumption” on November 1. Meanwhile, the explanation of the cause grew more complicated. At first, Binance pointed to a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer. Later, the company disclosed that its investigation had found more points of breach.
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida on October 31 that “we don’t know if it’s North Korea.” However, the FBI seems more sure. It previously blamed the same hacking operation, TraderTraitor, for the theft of about $1.5 billion from the exchange Bybit in February 2025. The Binance haul is more than four times as large as that sum.
Pyongyang has been building toward such a massive cyber heist for years. Over the past decade, North Korea has steadily built a hacking apparatus whose main purpose is to raise money for the Kim regime.
Back in 2019, the U.S. Treasury Department said that the Reconnaissance General Bureau, the main intelligence organization of North Korea, controls Lazarus Group, the name cybersecurity firms use for several North Korean hacking units. The Lazarus Group’s activities date back to at least 2007.
From the start, Lazarus Group built its reputation through disruption. In 2018 the Justice Department charged a North Korean programmer named Park Jin Hyok in connection with the 2014 attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment, the 2017 WannaCry outbreak, and a 2016 bank theft in Bangladesh. In that last case, hackers used stolen credentials to request $851 million in transfers from the account of the central bank of Bangladesh at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. About $80 million went through before a typographical error alerted staff to stop the rest.
North Korea began to focus its hacking operations on cryptocurrency theft around 2017, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 countries that includes the United States, South Korea and Japan. As the monitoring team noted, (using the abbreviation of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea), “The DPRK employs its cyber capabilities to circumvent UN sanctions and generate revenue for the DPRK’s priorities, including the unlawful development of its WMD and ballistic missile programs.” Back in 2017, North Korea faced a weak economy and tightening sanctions, and the young crypto industry lacked mature security. So the motive and the opportunity lined up.
Between 2016 and 2017 the Reconnaissance General Bureau formed a specialized team to steal cryptocurrency after earlier hacking units had succeeded against banks and the SWIFT system. Researchers once called that North Korean hacking team APT38 or Bluenoroff. But the monitoring team now says that it comprises two groups called TraderTraitor and CryptoCore. TraderTraitor is the actor that the FBI linked to both Bybit and Binance.
For TraderTraitor, a cyber attack usually begins by seeking entry to a single employee computer. In 2022, the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and the Treasury Department warned that the group sends large numbers of spearphishing messages to employees of crypto companies – usually system administrators and software developers. Spearphishing involves sending targeted messages that look personal and trustworthy. In practice, the messages often imitated a recruitment effort and offered high-paying jobs.
The attack on Bybit in February 2025 followed that script. The hackers posed as recruiters and sent a developer at the wallet provider Safe{Wallet} a fake pre-employment test that carried malicious code. The test likely gave them access to the internal network of the company. Using that access, on February 21 they altered the screen where Bybit users give approval for transfers. The users thought that they were approving a routine transfer; in fact, they were handing control of an offline wallet of the exchange to the hackers.
The original explanation offered by Binance – that a single infected computer started the attack – fits the same pattern. Binance and Bybit aren’t the only victims, either. Since mid-2024, TraderTraitor has targeted outside companies that hold keys for crypto exchanges. Those attacks produced at least $2 billion in thefts from Bybit, DMM Bitcoin in Japan, and WazirX in India, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team.
The thefts in 2024 alone totaled at least $1.19 billion – equivalent to about one-third of the foreign currency earnings of North Korea that year, according to the monitoring team. And that figure only includes hacks that could be attributed to North Korea with near certainty. The real total may be higher.
The Binance theft involved more than $6 billion. That’s over twice as much, in a single heist, as the total stolen from January 2024 to September 2025.
Of course, stealing the coins is only half of the work; the attackers must then withdraw the funds. The hackers obscure the money trail with mixers, bridges, and decentralized exchanges. In short, these services shuffle coins across accounts and networks. Then brokers in third countries turn the coins into cash.
The monitoring team noted that all of the money from Bybit had been converted into cash or hard currency by September 2025, about seven months after the original hack. In the Binance case the FBI observed that the hackers converted most of the stolen assets into Ethereum, likely as a first step to further laundering through decentralized finance and instant swap services.
The stage that turns stolen coins into spendable money relies heavily on China. The monitoring team found that North Korea used at least 15 Chinese banks to launder funds from heists and information technology (IT) work. North Korean units also depended on over-the-counter traders in China to convert stolen coins into cash.
China’s involvement goes beyond banking services. The Korea Herald, one of the main Korean newspapers reporting news in English, reported that Chinese nationals supplied forged identification documents to North Korean cyber groups. North Korean units used UnionPay cards and commercial banks in China to convert the proceeds into cash. Also, North Korea keeps 1,000 to 1,500 IT workers in China who earn foreign currency for the state. Then in September, the monitoring team noted that a North Korean diplomatic mission in China had reportedly cashed out stolen cryptocurrency through Chinese collaborators as of November 2025.
Beijing has applied pressure in some places. The monitoring team added that tighter anti-money-laundering checks at Chinese banks and crackdowns on illegal brokers had made the old money-exchange routes harder. Also, Chinese authorities have stepped up surveillance of North Korean IT workers. Chinese public security officers reportedly detained one such worker in April 2025 for allegedly stealing Chinese military secrets.
Governments involved in the monitoring team gave Beijing most of the China-related information in the 2025 report during 2024, and that information included the identities of North Korean and Chinese nationals involved in the illegal activities.
Nevertheless, loopholes remain. China remains the main hub where stolen coins become cash. In September, the monitoring team still described China as the primary hub for money laundering. In fact, China reportedly began to issue more trainee, student, and border-crossing visas to North Koreans after a diplomatic thaw in 2025. Past precedent shows that North Korean IT workers – and hackers – often enter China on trainee or student visas.
In short, Beijing has tightened the checks that protect its own banks from secondary sanctions, but Pyongyang keeps a working cash-out route inside China. Beijing has yet to face any real consequences for its enabling role.
Therefore the response to the Binance theft will test a weak point. The FBI has asked private companies to block transactions that involve listed Ethereum addresses. However, a block works only where the company at the end of the chain cooperates. Thus, the weak points are the brokers and banks that sit outside the reach of the FBI. Until Beijing closes the exits that remain, the next record theft is likely to still wind up in North Korea’s state coffers.

Palantir forecasts strong quarterly revenue on AI demand
Nov 2 : Palantir Technologies forecast revenue above estimates for the last three months of the year after topping third-quarter expectations, banking on sustained demand for its data-analytics software from the US government and commercial clients.
The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to be between $2.649 billion and $2.653 billion, it said on Monday, above LSEG-compiled analysts' average estimate of $2.46 billion.
However, shares fell nearly 3 per cent in extended trading.
"On the negative side, some investors may be disappointed with the US commercial bookings," William Blair analysts said.
The growth in US commercial total contract value – the potential lifetime value of signed contracts – slowed to 11 per cent year-over-year in the third quarter, from more than 153 per cent in the previous quarter.
Palantir said it signed multiple eight-figure deals in the quarter that were "shorter in duration than usual" as customers rapidly adopted initial sovereign AI capabilities, which allow enterprises to retain control over their data and how AI is deployed and used.
In the third quarter, revenue from commercial clients surpassed government revenue in the US for the first time, driven by the rapid adoption of AI software to improve operations and safeguard sensitive data.
Palantir, which develops the Maven Smart System used by NATO's military headquarters and several European armed forces, built its business around government and defense contracts.
Total quarterly revenue jumped about 96 per cent to $2.31 billion, the second straight quarter of 90 per cent growth. Analysts had estimated revenue of $2.18 billion.
US commercial revenue was $984 million, while US government revenue came in at $953 million during the period.
The company reported a total of 1,090 customers in the trailing 12-month period ending September 30, with 904 classified as commercial.
Palantir also raised its annual revenue expectations to between $8.530 billion and $8.534 billion, up from its prior estimates of between $8.150 billion and $8.158 billion.

India's startup funding market is undergoing a correction, with late-stage and angel investments declining sharply as global investors turn more selective and redirect capital towards other markets and sectors.
Rupee depreciation and intensifying competition, particularly from the US, have made fundraising harder for Indian startups and venture capital (VC) funds. Investors are also reassessing valuations and demanding stronger business fundamentals before committing capital.
The slowdown follows an exceptional funding boom in 2020 and 2021, which experts attribute to excessive liquidity and valuations that proved difficult to sustain.
Late-stage funding, which peaked at $29.7 billion in 2021, fell to $6.1 billion in 2025 and $5.7 billion as of 26 October 2026. The number of rounds also declined from 277 in 2021 to 164 in 2025 and 98 so far in 2026, according to Tracxn data.
“As interest rates normalized, capital rebalanced and the market reset to levels that fundamentals could support. What has changed is the underwriting discipline. The anchor is now public-market comparables, which means positive unit economics, a clear path to profitability, improving contribution margins and cash conversion,” said Karan Mohla, general partner at global multi-stage venture capital firm B Capital, where he leads the South and Southeast Asia team.
Analysts view the decline as a re-baselining of the ecosystem. The 2021 peak was driven by the zero interest rate policy (ZIRP) era, when abundant capital flowed into late-stage private rounds at forward revenue multiples that public markets were unlikely to sustain.
A changing landscape
A shift in investor appetite is adding to the slowdown. While funds earlier backed conventional financial services and internet businesses, interest has increasingly moved towards artificial intelligence (AI) and deeptech. Many companies in these sectors, however, are still too young to attract late-stage investments.
“My sense is that late-stage funding will pick up around 2028, when these companies mature and graduate to that stage. Until then, some companies in the consumer and financial services sectors will continue to attract late-stage capital. However, the investment landscape is undergoing a reset, with a shift in the kinds of businesses investors find attractive,” said Ashish Kumar, co-founder and general partner at venture capital firm Fundamentum and F2A (Fundamentum Frontier Advisors).
Between 2020 and 2026 YTD, retail, enterprise applications and fintech attracted the most funding, at $32.2 billion, $31.5 billion and $25.6 billion, respectively, Tracxn data showed.
The retreat of once-active growth-stage investors has further constrained capital flows. Tiger Global's investments in Indian startups fell from 55 in 2021 to one in 2026 YTD. SoftBank, which made 17 investments in 2021, largely stayed away from fresh deals after 2022 before making two investments in 2026, according to Venture Intelligence.
Global capital looks elsewhere
Competition from the US has added to the pressure, with global investors increasingly concentrating capital in artificial intelligence. Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have raised billions of dollars at multi-billion-dollar valuations. SpaceX's entry into public markets through its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) in June has added to the pull of the US technology market.
“As a result, there is little incentive for an LP to invest in VC funds in India right now. India has become a classic high-potential but underperforming market for global LPs,” said Abhay Agarwal, founder and fund manager of early-stage VC firm Piper Serica Advisors.
The pullback extends to the earliest stages of startup financing. Angel funding ffell from $542 million in 2020 to $95.4 million in 2025, while the number of rounds declined from 577 to 286, according to Traxcn data.
Experts attribute the decline partly to the growing institutionalisation of angel investing. Angel networks are increasingly setting up their own funds, tapping domestic capital to formalise early-stage investments in the startup ecosystem, Mint reported in March.
Regulatory changes have added to the uncertainty. Under revisions to the Securities and Exchange Board of India's (Sebi) accredited investor framework, angel funds can raise capital only from accredited investors and must onboard at least five such investors before their first close. Investors must meet prescribed income or net-worth criteria and undergo accreditation.
The changes have raised concerns that smaller and newer fund managers could struggle to raise capital, as the requirements narrow the pool of eligible investors. Following industry representations, Sebi extended the compliance deadline for existing angel funds from 8 September 2026 to 31 March 2027.
However, some industry participants argue that tighter regulations may change how angel capital is deployed rather than reduce its overall availability.
“If getting accredited is too onerous or the eligible pool shrinks too much, you'll see capital simply route around the regulated structure — people will invest directly or find other vehicles. So the regulation may end up reshaping the pipeline more than shrinking the overall pool,” said Nidhi Killawala, partner at law firm Khaitan & Co.

indian-startups-8a00b72125.headline: Health-tech startup Clinics On Cloud raises $12.5 Mn in Series A round
indian-startups-8a00b72125.fulltext:
Pune-based health-tech startup Clinics On Cloud has raised $12.5 million in a Series A funding round from Dubai-based investors through Model42, powered by Enlightened Minds Investments.
The fresh funds will be used to strengthen its artificial intelligence (AI)-led healthcare capabilities, expand research and development (R&D), and grow its connected microclinic network, Clinics On Cloud said in a press release.
The funding will also support the company’s international expansion, with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) serving as its global expansion hub. The company plans to explore opportunities across Africa, the United States and Southeast Asia.
Clinics On Cloud also plans to establish partnerships with healthcare providers, technology companies and organisations seeking to deploy connected microclinics across different markets.
Founded in 2018 by Abhay Agarwal, Clinics On Cloud develops technology-enabled healthcare infrastructure focused on preventive healthcare. The company has recorded over 3,500 deployments and conducted more than 12 million health screenings across eight countries.
Initially focused on Health ATMs, the company has expanded its portfolio to include Health Lounges, Box Clinics and Mobile Medical Units. Its solutions combine preventive health screening, AI-assisted health insights and telemedicine to enable hospitals, pharmacies, healthcare entrepreneurs, corporates and government organisations to establish microclinics across workplaces, housing societies, malls and underserved communities.
The company’s infrastructure has been deployed across government health centres, hospitals, corporate campuses and rural communities, as well as Indian defence establishments, including the Army, Navy and Border Security Force (BSF).
Clinics On Cloud also plans to collaborate with global healthcare innovators to integrate AI and advanced screening technologies into its platform.

indian-startups-98ee6f643b.headline: After 8 bootstrapped years, Health ATM maker Clinics On Cloud raises Rs 120 crore at Rs 600 crore valuation
indian-startups-98ee6f643b.fulltext:
Pune-based healthtech startup Clinics On Cloud has raised Rs 120 crore (about $12.5 million) in a Series A funding round from Dubai-based investors through Model42, a healthcare investment platform powered by Enlightened Minds Investments.
The round values the startup at Rs 600 crore.
Clinics On Cloud makes Health ATMs, self-service kiosks that run preventive health check-ups, along with other formats for what it calls connected microclinics. The company announced the round last week.
Notably, it is the startup's first institutional funding. Clinics On Cloud was founded in 2018 by Abhay Agarwal and Manashrri Agarwal and grew without outside capital for eight years before this round.
"For eight years, we have built Clinics On Cloud with a simple belief that quality healthcare should never depend on someone's PIN code," said Abhay Agarwal, Founder and CEO of Clinics On Cloud.
"This investment gives us the opportunity to take that vision global. Healthcare technology is advancing rapidly, but the real opportunity is making these innovations accessible to people, wherever they are. That's the infrastructure we want to build," he added.
Where the money will go
The startup plans to use the funds to strengthen its AI-led healthcare capabilities, expand research and development, and grow its network of connected microclinics. It has also said the capital will go towards international regulatory compliance and scaling up manufacturing of its devices.
The UAE will serve as its global expansion hub, from where it plans to pursue opportunities in Africa, the United States and Southeast Asia.
The funding will also support partnerships with healthcare providers, technology companies and organisations that want to set up connected microclinics in different markets. Clinics On Cloud said it plans to work with global healthcare innovators to add emerging AI and advanced screening technologies to its platform, so that these tools can be used outside traditional healthcare settings.
What Clinics On Cloud does
According to the company's website, its Health ATM carries out a preventive screening in about 10 minutes and can check more than 65 clinical parameters, depending on the model. These include blood pressure, blood sugar, ECG and other cardiac, diabetes and pulmonary measurements. The kiosks are voice-guided and multilingual, work offline, do not need skilled staff to run, and send reports over WhatsApp or email, with teleconsultation built in.
The startup describes itself as a CDSCO-licensed Health ATM manufacturer. Its manufacturing facility is at Chakan MIDC near Pune.
Having started with Health ATMs, it has added Health Lounges, which are wellness screening spaces for offices and communities, Box Clinics, which are portable units for rural camps and outreach, and Mobile Medical Units. Together, these let hospitals, pharmacies, healthcare entrepreneurs, companies and government bodies set up microclinics in workplaces, housing societies, malls and underserved areas.
Clinics On Cloud claims to have more than 3,500 deployments, has carried out over 12 million health screenings, and operates in more than 8 countries, including UAE, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Madagascar, Nigeria, Kenya, Ivory Coast and the Philippines. Notably, In India it covers more than 200 Indian cities.
Some of its notable clients named on its website include Reliance, Tata Power, Godrej, Bajaj Allianz and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, along with AIIMS Rishikesh.
How it started
Agarwal has written on his personal website that the idea came to him in 2017, when he asked why a basic health check could not be as easy as withdrawing cash from an ATM. He spent 2018 and 2019 on research and experimentation with no external funding or large team, and launched commercially in 2020.
The first big order came that year from a government body, for 100 units, which took a full year to execute, according to Agarwal.

india-deep-tech-95a384f9d4.headline: Robotics startup Tutor Intelligence nabs $75M investment
india-deep-tech-95a384f9d4.fulltext:
Robotics startup Tutor Intelligence nabs $75M investment
Warehouse automation provider Tutor Intelligence Inc. today announced that it has raised $75 million in funding.
Andreessen Horowitz led the Series A investment. It was joined by Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led Tutor’s previous two rounds.
The merchandise that a warehouse processes often arrives on pallets, flat wood structures capable of holding up to several tons. Tutor sells a mobile robotic arm called Cassie that can take packages off a pallet and place them in containers. It’s also capable of performing the opposite operation.
Cassie can process up to 18 items per minute depending on the package type. Its robotic arm is equipped with a vacuum gripper designed to pick up more than 50 pounds. The arm is mounted on a four-wheeled platform that enables Cassie to autonomously travel between different sections of a warehouse.
Automating pallet processing is challenging because the merchandise that a warehouse receives changes over time. Historically, adapting a robotic arm’s workflow to a new item involved manual coding. Cassie uses built-in artificial intelligence models to learn how to pick up new package types automatically.
Tutor also ships its AI models with a second wheeled robot called Sonny. It uses a pair of robotic arms to take items off warehouse shelves and place them in packages. The robot finds the needed items using an array of time-of-flight and stereo cameras. Both camera varieties collect depth data, which makes it easier to determine the distance of an object.
Tutor plans to apply Sonny to additional use cases in the future. In particular, it sees industrial companies using the system to assemble products and perform equipment maintenance. Tutor teaches Sonny’s AI models new tasks in a facility that hosts more than 100 robots. Human experts demonstrate how to perform a task using a remotely controlled robot and the AI models learn by imitation.
“Sonny’s manufacturability at scale makes it an ideal robot not just for most handwork in manufacturing and logistics, but for arbitrary business-critical applications across the physical economy,” Tutor co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Josh Gruenstein wrote in a blog post. “Data collected by our Sonny fleet trains our largest and most capable robot foundation models at the frontier of rate and reliability.”
Tutor sells its robots under a usage-based pricing model. It removes the need for customers to make a large upfront purchase, which lowers the entry barrier. The company disclosed today that the number of facilities where its robots are used has nearly quadrupled over the past year.
Tutor will use its newly raised funding to enhance its AI models and speed up robot production.
